rationale: A bare macro token in FIELD position makes the grammar promote it to a type_identifier, and the parse comes out as field_declaration{ type_identifier(TSD_DATA_SLOW) field_identifier(tsd_state_t) ';' MISSING } followed by field_declaration{ type_identifier(state) ';' }. The extractor then published the TYPE as a member of tsd_s -- a symbol a reader can navigate to that resolves to nothing. Measured: 1 occurrence over the 2,498-file curl+libgit2+redis corpus (redis/deps/jemalloc/include/jemalloc/internal/tsd.h:255). The construct is legal C: the preprocessor does not care about braces, so a #define inside a struct body and a macro token where a field belongs are both fine. #932 SUPPRESSES the phantom and does NOT MEND the real member. `state` is one token away in the next declaration's type slot, and a two-token mend whose generality was not measured is exactly the fabrication recovery risks; so the loss of `state` is declared rather than invented. The trade is deliberate: a phantom member is a symbol that exists and is wrong, which is worse than a member that is absent and recorded as absent. The two controls are what make the rule sound rather than a shape heuristic. `struct type_named_member { struct S S; }` is LEGAL C -- the declarator is an ordinary identifier while the tag lives in its own namespace -- so a member may share a spelling with a type declared in the same file, and only the MISSING ';' (which well-formed C never produces) separates that case from the defect. The `define_only` control is the #define-inside-a-struct shape with a well-formed field after it, which must change nothing.

expectSymbols.name: S
expectSymbols.note: CONTROL: a member may LEGALLY share a spelling with a type in the same file. The struct here is a FORWARD declaration (`struct S;` with no body), so it is deliberately NOT a symbol -- a reference declaration is not a definition site -- and what the control pins is that the MEMBER named after it still lands with its containment.
